verdict_a: BLOCK, narrowly and cheaply. THE DECISION IS AFFIRMED AND THE SENTENCE IS REFUSED. Three things are separable here and I rule on them separately. (1) THE OWNER'S RULING THAT THE DESCRIPTION GETS ITS OWN CLAIM RATHER THAN A COMPRESSION OF AN EXISTING ONE IS CORRECT, and the stated reasoning survives scrutiny: claims.render_surface emits each claim's limitations as sub-bullets under its wording, so on `README`, `report` and `abstract` the limitations DO travel mechanically; a GitHub description field takes one string and can receive no sub-bullets. That is a structural difference in this repository's own rendering model, not a rationalisation, and it means a claim written for `abstract` genuinely cannot be trimmed into a description without dropping the half the claim boundaries protect. (2) THE `repo_description` SURFACE IS CORRECT IN PRINCIPLE and is not surface proliferation, subject to A6. (3) THE WORDING AND THE `method` FIELD ARE BLOCKED. The `method` field splices a figure to the wrong source: it attributes '~16x grounding separation' to CX-GROUNDING-01, whose approved wording never contains the phrase; '~16x grounding gain' is CX-GROUNDING-ORTHOGONAL-01's wording, that claim is `qualified` not `verified`, and docs/plan3/certification-result.md licenses the ~16x figure in the ADR-0011 bullet with the words 'Reported with the restricted-population caveat attached' -- a caveat none of the four limitations carries. Taking a number from one claim and its citation from another is the exact defect class REVIEW.md's new 'Cite one source per figure' gate was added to catch, IN THIS COMMIT, three files away. A reviewer who waved that through one commit after the repository elevated it to a gate would not be ruling adversarially. Compounding it: the wording attributes the null to QLoRA when the null is all three systems, on the one surface where the limitation saying so cannot travel; and `verified_by` states 'Routed for independent review' while the claim carries a public surface, escaping PENDING_VERIFICATION_TRIPWIRE only through the leading-token anchoring that claims.py documents as a known gap. BLOCK is proportionate because it is cheap: nothing is published, the field is empty, the repository is private, and every required item is a string edit. A1-A7 discharge to PASS with no new measurement, no new science and no re-review of the ledger.

overclaiming_the_null_column.presenting_a_diagnostic_as_a_certificate: NO MATCH. Neither the alpha-frontier nor the grounding oracle is invoked.
overclaiming_the_null_column.claiming_we_discovered_crc_cannot_certif: NO MATCH. 'An evidence-first negative result' is a claim about this project's own outcome, not about the method's general capacity. Recorded as watched and cleared.

overclaiming_the_positive_column.95_7_quotable_without_the_null: NO MATCH AND CORRECTLY SO. 95.7 does not appear, in any form, and the decision document's own line -- '95.7% grounded event-argument extraction remains forbidden by name' -- is respected. This is the wording's best property and it should survive whatever replaces it.
overclaiming_the_positive_column.any_certified_margin: NO MATCH against the `certified (margin|advantage|gain)` pattern. But see A3: `certified coverage` is a phrase the pattern set does not contain and the project's own vocabulary does not use.
overclaiming_the_positive_column.calling_grounding_validity_accuracy: NO MATCH in the wording; limitation 3 states the distinction correctly. But the distinction cannot travel, and 'a ~16x grounding gain' standing alone is the phrase most likely to be read as a quality figure. See A2b.

does_bought_no_certified_coverage_state_.ruling: NO. It is weaker than the record in two directions, and on a surface where nothing can correct it.
does_bought_no_certified_coverage_state_.a2a_it_narrows_the_null_to_qlora: The sentence's subject is 'a ~16x grounding gain from QLoRA' and its predicate is 'bought no certified coverage'. A reader takes from that: QLoRA's gain failed to buy certification. The record is that NEITHER QLoRA NOR EITHER BASELINE could be certified -- CX-H1-PRIMARY is `infeasible` for QA and ZS, CX-H2-SECONDARY likewise for FS, and docs/plan3/certification-result.md states 'H1 and H2 are both_infeasible' and 'There is one finding, not two.' The claim's OWN limitation 2 says exactly this -- '"No certified coverage" is the null for all three systems, not a QLoRA-versus-baseline comparison' -- and limitation 2 is the one limitation that CANNOT TRAVEL, because the whole premise of this surface is that limitations do not travel. So the wording, on the single surface with no second passage, encodes the precise misreading that its own limitation exists to prevent. That is the wrong way round: the field should carry the half that cannot be caveated, and caveat the half that can.
does_bought_no_certified_coverage_state_.a2a_why_this_is_not_pedantry: The misreading is not neutral. It makes the null look narrower and more QLoRA-specific than it is, i.e. it makes the result look LESS negative. CLAUDE.md's honesty boundary makes negative results first-class publishable outcomes; softening a null is a distortion in this project's terms even though the forbidden table's null column only enumerates OVER-claims of the null. The forbidden table does not catch it. That is a gap in the table, not a licence.
does_bought_no_certified_coverage_state_.a2b_it_reads_as_a_near_miss: 'Bought no X' is purchase framing: it presupposes X was on sale and implies a larger payment might have bought it. The record forecloses that. docs/plan3/certification-result.md: 'below alpha ~ 0.406 NO certificate at any threshold could have cleared the floor for the best system -- the entire range is ruled out without a certificate being computed anywhere in it', and CX-CAPGAP-01: with an unlimited grid, no finite-sample penalty and oracle selection, the adapted system accepts at most 2.0% against a required 20%. That is a factor of ten short under an oracle, not an unbought margin. 'Bought no certified coverage' is compatible with 'came close and fell short', and the record is 'was never reachable'. It does not IMPLY a margin, which is why this is a required rewrite and not a forbidden-table hit -- but it permits one, and permitting one is exactly what a surface with no second passage must not do.
does_bought_no_certified_coverage_state_.the_one_thing_it_gets_right_and_it_matte: THE GAIN AND THE NULL ARE IN THE SAME SENTENCE, joined by a verb that makes the null the outcome of the gain. That satisfies the boundary rule literally and in spirit. Whatever replaces this wording must keep that construction; it is the hardest part of the problem and the author solved it.

does_the_16x_survive_the_same_passage_ru.ruling: THE SAME-PASSAGE RULE IS SATISFIED. A DIFFERENT RULE IS NOT.
does_the_16x_survive_the_same_passage_ru.same_passage: Yes. 'a ~16x grounding gain from QLoRA bought no certified coverage' is one clause. The gain cannot be quoted from this field without the null coming with it, which is what docs/plan3/certification-result.md requires when it permits the Plan 2 grounding result 'in the same document and the same passage as the null'. There is no way to excerpt half of this sentence and leave a grammatical claim.
does_the_16x_survive_the_same_passage_ru.the_rule_that_is_not_satisfied: docs/plan3/certification-result.md permits the ~16x figure in exactly one place -- the ADR 0011 bullet, 'a ~16x grounding gain moved the certifiable frontier by +0.017 for QA and by 0.000 for both baselines, with 87% of QA's residual loss in grounded, content-bearing output' -- and closes it with 'Reported with the restricted-population caveat attached.' The corresponding ledger claim CX-GROUNDING-ORTHOGONAL-01 carries that caveat in terms: 'Conditional coverage under the grounding oracle is not a deployable acceptance rate and is not comparable across systems; the restricted population differs per system.' CX-REPO-DESCRIPTION-01 quotes the figure and carries no such caveat. There is a DEFENSIBLE reading on which the caveat attaches to the +0.017 and the 87% rather than to the ~16x ratio itself, and the new claim quotes neither of those -- but the claim's `method` field does not make that argument, does not identify which permitted bullet licenses the figure, and instead cites the wrong claim entirely. See A1.
does_the_16x_survive_the_same_passage_ru.a2b_what_16x_actually_measures: A separate and more serious problem for a standalone field. The grounding RATE went 39.4% (ZS) to 95.7% (QA): a factor of 2.4. The ~16x is the reduction in UNGROUNDED spans, 5,355 to 340 = 15.75x. A reader of a bare description will take '~16x grounding gain' to mean grounding improved sixteenfold, overstating the rate improvement by about 6.6x. The phrase is reviewer-approved wording in CX-GROUNDING-ORTHOGONAL-01, so the description did not invent it -- but there it sits beside '+0.017 for itself and 0.000 for both baselines' and '87% of its remaining loss', which anchor it. Standalone, nothing anchors it. This is the strongest argument for the numberless replacement offered in question 5.

question_2_is_repo_description_a_correct.ruling: CORRECT IN PRINCIPLE, UNDER-DELIVERED IN CODE. The distinction is real and I can point at the mechanism that makes it real; the author's stated reason is not a rationalisation. But the surface as added enforces nothing, and the comment above it reads as though it does.
question_2_is_repo_description_a_correct.why_the_distinction_is_real_and_the_auth: The author argues from the abstract's room for limitations. The stronger form is in this repository's own code and the author did not cite it: claims.render_surface renders each claim as `- [ID] wording` followed by `  - _Limitation:_ ...` for every limitation. On `README`, `report` and `abstract` the limitations therefore travel MECHANICALLY -- docs/writeup/claims-appendix.generated.md is the artifact, generated for surface `report`, and every claim in it carries its limitations as sub-bullets. A GitHub description field accepts one string and cannot receive a sub-bullet. So the difference between `abstract` and `repo_description` is not an editorial judgement about how much room a genre has; it is the difference between a surface the renderer can protect and one it cannot. That is a structural distinction in the project's own model and it fully answers the rationalisation charge.
question_2_is_repo_description_a_correct.is_it_proliferation: NO on the merits. PUBLIC_SURFACES had eight members covering seven genres plus `abstract`; a ninth for a genre that exists, is public, and has a different rendering contract is not drift. The permanence objection -- adding a surface widens PUBLIC_SURFACES forever -- is real but weak here: the set is a validation whitelist, and the cost of an unused member is zero while the cost of a claim written for the wrong surface is what this whole item exists to prevent. The genuine proliferation risk would be a surface added to make ONE awkward wording legal. That is not what happened: the surface was added because the constraint is different, and the wording was then authored for the constraint. The order of reasoning is the right one.

a6_the_defect_that_does_need_fixing.what: `repo_description` is a bare string in a frozenset. Nothing distinguishes it from `abstract` at runtime. There is no length bound, no rule that its claims must be self-contained, and -- the concrete one -- `render_surface(ledger, 'repo_description')` will happily emit `- [CX-REPO-DESCRIPTION-01] <wording>` followed by four `  - _Limitation:_` lines, which is not a string anyone can paste into the field. The renderer does not know this surface is different, which is the entire justification for the surface existing.
a6_the_defect_that_does_need_fixing.why_it_matters_beyond_tidiness: The docstring above PUBLIC_SURFACES now asserts a distinction ('an abstract has room to carry a claim's limitations in the same passage; a repository description is one line with no second passage') that the code does not implement. A comment that describes a protection the code does not provide is the shape of defect this repository has recorded three times over: a sentence whose scope exceeds what produced it. It is worse here than in prose, because a reader of claims.py will reasonably infer the constraint is enforced.
acceptable_discharges_either_is_fine: ENFORCE IT: give `repo_description` a maximum wording length (350, GitHub's limit) and a validator rule that a claim carrying it must state its scope inside the wording, with a test. This is the stronger option and is a small change to Claim.validate_claim.

DISCLAIM IT: amend the docstring to say in terms that the surface is a documentation marker enforcing nothing at runtime, that render_surface's limitation sub-bullets are not pasteable into the field, and that the one-line constraint is held by review rather than by code. This costs nothing and removes the false implication.

question_3_are_the_four_limitations_adeq.limitation_1_in_domain_rams_frozen_opera: ADEQUATE AND HONEST, and the best of the four. It names alpha 0.20, delta 0.05, the 0.20 acceptance floor and the vLLM 4-bit stack, then says 'None of that fits in the field, which is why the field must not be read as the claim's scope.' That last clause is doing real work: it tells a future reader that the field is not the claim's scope statement, which is the correct relationship between a description and a ledger entry. Keep verbatim.
question_3_are_the_four_limitations_adeq.limitation_2_the_null_is_for_all_three_s: HONEST AND CORRECT, AND IN THE WRONG PLACE. It is right that the null is all three systems and that H1/H2 collapse to one finding. But it is stated as a caveat to a wording that says the opposite, on the one surface where caveats do not travel. A limitation is 'a condition that must travel with the claim' (accepted plan section 3.4); this one cannot, by the surface's definition. The fix is not to strengthen the limitation -- it is to move its content into the wording, which is what question 5's replacement does. Once the wording says 'no system -- QLoRA, few-shot or zero-shot', limitation 2 becomes a supporting note rather than a correction.
question_3_are_the_four_limitations_adeq.limitation_3_grounding_gain_is_not_corre: ADEQUATE AND MANDATORY. It restates CX-GROUNDING-01's own limitation and the forbidden table's 'Calling grounding validity accuracy'. Its capitals ('NOT correctness') are earned. Keep. Note that it becomes less load-bearing under the numberless replacement and MORE load-bearing if the owner keeps a figure, which is an argument for the numberless form.

limitation_4_the_description_is_a_pointe.ruling: SELF-SOOTHING AS WRITTEN. It is doing rhetorical work for the surface's legitimacy, not conditional work on the claim, and its one factual sentence quantifies over the wrong population.
limitation_4_the_description_is_a_pointe.the_sentence: 'Every figure behind it lives in the ledger and the certification record, and a reader arriving from the description reaches those before any number.'
limitation_4_the_description_is_a_pointe.why_it_fails: The clause is true of readers who ARRIVE. The decision document's own framing of why a description matters is that it 'is rendered on every search result, every listing, and every link preview' -- that is, the population the field exists to reach is overwhelmingly the population that reads it and does NOT click. The limitation therefore establishes something about the readers who do not need the protection and nothing about the readers who do. It is the scope-matches-sentence failure in miniature: a reassuring universal ('a reader ... reaches those before any number') resting on a mechanism that covers a subset.
limitation_4_the_description_is_a_pointe.and_it_is_not_a_limitation: 'The description is a pointer to the result, not the result' is a framing note about the genre, not a condition that travels with the claim. A limitation field populated with an argument for why the claim is safe is the field being used to hold its own defence. The three real limitations above are conditions; this one is comfort.
limitation_4_the_description_is_a_pointe.what_would_do_real_work_instead: A binding condition on reuse: 'This wording is approved for the GitHub repository description field only. It may not be reused on any surface where a caveat could have travelled -- README, report, abstract, card, CV or slide -- where the fuller claims (CX-H1-PRIMARY, CX-GROUNDING-01, CX-GROUNDING-ORTHOGONAL-01) govern and their limitations must appear.' That is a condition, it is checkable, and it closes the real risk, which is this compressed sentence leaking onto a surface that could have afforded the caveats.

question_3_are_the_four_limitations_adeq.what_is_missing_from_the_set: One candidate, recorded rather than required: if the owner keeps a figure in the wording, the set needs a limitation naming which quantity ~16x is (the reduction in ungrounded spans, 5,355 to 340), because the ratio is not the grounding-rate ratio (2.4x) and the two are six-fold apart. Under the numberless replacement this is unnecessary, which is one more reason to prefer it.

does_status_negative_fit.ruling: DEFENSIBLE, NOT OBVIOUSLY RIGHT, AND NOTHING TURNS ON IT MECHANICALLY. I am not requiring a change.
does_status_negative_fit.for_negative: docs/plan3/certification-result.md's own Status section calls the result 'A first-class publishable negative result', and CLAUDE.md's honesty boundary uses the same word. Both `negative` and `infeasible` are in PROSE_PERMITTED, so publishability is unaffected either way.
does_status_negative_fit.against_negative: The operative half of the sentence -- 'bought no certified coverage' -- is the finding the ledger already holds as `infeasible` (CX-H1-PRIMARY, CX-H2-SECONDARY, CX-CAPGAP-01 are the three `infeasible` entries). `negative` reads as 'we tested X and it did not help'; `infeasible` reads as 'no certificate could issue'. The second is what happened. Choosing the softer word is consistent with A2b's near-miss reading, and the two together are a pattern rather than two coincidences.
does_status_negative_fit.the_finding_underneath: THE LEDGER HAS NO REPRESENTATION FOR A COMPOSITE CLAIM. CX-REPO-DESCRIPTION-01 conjoins a `verified` claim (CX-GROUNDING-01) or a `qualified` one (CX-GROUNDING-ORTHOGONAL-01) with an `infeasible` one (CX-H1-PRIMARY), and the schema offers one enum slot. There is no composed-from field, no way for verify-claims to check that a composite's parts are themselves publishable, and no way for a later reader to see the composition except by reading `method` prose -- which, in this instance, is wrong. That is a schema gap the arrival of this claim exposes. Recorded as A7, non-blocking, and worth an ADR if any second composite claim is ever written.

is_verified_by_honest.ruling: THE PROSE IS HONEST. THE FIELD IS NOT DOING WHAT THE GATE NEEDS IT TO DO.
is_verified_by_honest.why_the_prose_is_honest: It says 'Composed 2026-07-29 from two claims already independently reviewed', names both with their review dates (CX-GROUNDING-01 reconciled 2026-07-21, CX-H1-PRIMARY reviewer PASS 2026-07-22), and does not claim a new measurement. Composing reviewed claims rather than measuring something new is the right basis for this entry and saying so plainly is correct. I looked for a concealed assertion of fresh verification and there is none.
is_verified_by_honest.a5_the_defect: The same field continues: 'Routed for independent review as a new public sentence; the repository is private and the field is empty, so nothing is published by this entry.' So the claim carries a public surface while its own verification record states that its review has not happened. That is the exact regression PENDING_VERIFICATION_TRIPWIRE was written for after ADR 0011 -- and it passes, because the tripwire is anchored to the leading token and this string opens with 'Composed'. claims.py documents the anchoring and lists eleven strings it misses; 'Routed for independent review' is a twelfth, and it is the first one to appear in the ledger rather than in a test corpus. The honest prose is what defeats the gate: a vaguer field ('reviewed') would have passed cleanly and said less. That is the pressure-toward-vagueness the anchoring comment warns about, arriving in production.
is_verified_by_honest.what_i_am_not_saying: I am NOT requiring the tripwire be widened. claims.py argues, with a measured corpus, that an unanchored form penalises detailed provenance records and rewards the word 'reviewed', and that argument is sound and I am not reopening it. The fix is to the field, not the regex.
is_verified_by_honest.required: A5. On discharge, `verified_by` must record THIS review's outcome and date rather than asserting that review is pending. If the owner discharges A1-A4 and sets the field, the ledger must not be left permanently saying a completed review is outstanding -- which is itself a document asserting a gate state that its own records contradict, the defect class REVIEW.md holds three instances of.

constraints_i_wrote_against: One line. GitHub accepts 350 characters; the incumbent uses 152, so there is real headroom and brevity is not an excuse for dropping the null's scope.
The gain and the null must be in the same clause, and the null must not be quotable without the gain or the gain without the null. The incumbent achieves this and any replacement must too.
The null belongs to all three systems. A description that attributes it to QLoRA alone reports a softer result than the record.
No 95.7, forbidden by name. No alpha value, and no wording that leaves the operating point unnamed in a way that invites a reader to imagine a different one.
Any figure must be the quantity it appears to be, or must not appear.

preferred_replacement.wording: Selective, grounded event-argument extraction on RAMS: QLoRA sharply improved grounding, and no system - QLoRA, few-shot or zero-shot - could be certified at the frozen risk target. An evidence-first negative result.
why_this_one: 'no system - QLoRA, few-shot or zero-shot - could be certified' states the null at its true breadth in the wording, so limitation 2 no longer has to travel and no longer fails to.

'could be certified' is CX-H1-PRIMARY's own reviewed verb and removes 'coverage' (A3). 'Could not' is a modal of impossibility, which is what the alpha-frontier established; 'bought no' was a modal of transaction, which is not.

'at the frozen risk target' names the operating point as fixed-in-advance without quoting a number. It is a positive block on the laxer-alpha reading rather than mere silence, and it is accurate: ADR 0007 froze it before any sealed label was opened.

'sharply improved grounding' keeps the gain, keeps it in the same clause as the null, and removes the ~16x -- which dissolves A1's citation problem, the restricted-population caveat question, and the six-fold misreading of what the ratio measures, all at once. The permitted list PERMITS reporting the gain; it does not require a number, and a number that needs a caveat is the wrong thing to put on the one surface that cannot carry one.
'evidence-first negative result' is kept verbatim from the incumbent. It is good, it is the project's own framing, and it is the phrase a reader most needs to see.

acceptable_alternative_if_the_owner_want.wording: Selective, grounded event-argument extraction on RAMS: QLoRA cut ungrounded spans ~16x, and no system - QLoRA, few-shot or zero-shot - could be certified at the frozen risk target. An evidence-first negative result.
acceptable_alternative_if_the_owner_want.why_it_is_acceptable: 'cut ungrounded spans ~16x' is precisely what the ratio measures (5,355 to 340 = 15.75x), it is stated verbatim in CX-GROUNDING-01's approved wording so the citation is then correct, that claim is `verified`, and the ADR-0011 restricted-population caveat does not attach because no oracle quantity is quoted. It cannot be read as accuracy and it cannot be read as a sixteenfold grounding rate. If the owner wants a number, this is the number to use and this is how to say it.
acceptable_alternative_if_the_owner_want.why_it_is_second_choice: Any figure on a caveat-free surface is a standing liability, and 'ungrounded spans' is jargon that a search-result reader will not parse. The preferred form loses nothing a reader of a one-line field can actually use.

question_5_a_better_wording.what_i_am_not_proposing_and_why: I did not attempt a wording that keeps '~16x grounding gain' and adds a restricted-population clause. It does not fit honestly in one line, and forcing it produces a sentence that is technically complete and unreadable, which on a search-result surface is not a better outcome than a shorter true one. If the owner disagrees and wants the ORTHOGONAL-01 framing, that is a different claim and should be routed as one.

question_6_is_the_central_question_well_.ruling: YES. IT IS WELL-POSED AND THE ACCEPTED PLAN DOES NOT SETTLE IT. Routing it separately was correct and it is not re-routed.
question_6_is_the_central_question_well_.what_section_17_says_in_primary_text: Two lists under one heading. 'Direction acceptance now' -- nine ticked boxes, the acceptance instrument itself. 'Evidence acceptance before public release' -- twelve unticked boxes. The phrase 'public release' appears only in that sub-heading and is never defined anywhere in the document. That is the whole of the ambiguity and it is real.

what_section_2_says_in_primary_text.2_1: The workflow ends '... licence, privacy and link audit -> public versioned release -> anonymous fresh-download verification', and 'Every quantitative public sentence maps to a claim ID and immutable artifacts.' The governed object is a RELEASE, and one audit node stands between draft and public. 2.1 does not mention repository visibility and does not exclude it either.
what_section_2_says_in_primary_text.2_2: Levels of reproducibility. Result replay is mandatory and is satisfiable inside the repository. Silent on visibility.
what_section_2_says_in_primary_text.2_3: Which OUTCOMES may support a release, and confirms 'all systems are infeasible' is one of them. Silent on visibility.

why_it_is_genuinely_open: THE WORD 'VISIBILITY' APPEARS NOWHERE IN THE ACCEPTED PLAN. Neither does 'private repository' or 'public repository' as a setting. Section 11's stage names are 'private/draft staging' and 'public canonical release', but R2's 'private' qualifies the Hugging Face candidates and the GitHub release DRAFT -- and a GitHub release draft is invisible whether the repository is public or private, so R2 does not require a private repository to make sense.

SECTION 11 R3 ENUMERATES FIVE PUBLISH ACTS and none of them is 'make the repository readable': publish tag/release and report; publish HF Dataset then adapter; publish/update the Collection; publish Kaggle Dataset and notebook; update cross-links. Section 5.1's ten steps are the same shape. A plan that meant to gate visibility had two natural places to say so and used neither.

BUT SECTION 3.1 NAMES THE REPOSITORY ITSELF AS A CANONICAL PUBLIC ARTIFACT: 'GitHub | `conformalextract` repository AND tagged release | source, tests, methods, report and canonical version history.' Not the release alone -- the repository. If the repository is a canonical public artifact, then making it readable is the publication of that artifact, and section 17's heading reaches it.

AND SECTION 12.4 PRESUPPOSES A PUBLIC REPOSITORY WITHOUT GATING ONE: 'pin ConformalExtract only after the public quickstart works' sits in portfolio consolidation, downstream of everything, and treats public visibility as a state the project will be in rather than an act the plan schedules.
question_6_is_the_central_question_well_.ruling_in_full: The accepted plan settles that a RELEASE is gated by section 17 and does not settle whether the ACT OF BECOMING READABLE is a release. Both readings have primary-text support -- 3.1 for the affirmative, 11 and 5.1 for the negative -- and neither is decisive. The prior reviewer's finding that 'visibility is not one of the seven items, is not mentioned in section 1, and appears nowhere in section 11's stages as a gated object' is correct as far as it goes, and the proposal is right that it stopped short of ruling. So this is a real question and it needed routing. My answer to it is question 10.
question_6_is_the_central_question_well_.one_correction_to_the_proposal_s_framing: The proposal writes that whether 'release' means the seven-item contribution or the act of becoming readable 'is the question the staged-release rejection turned on without settling'. That is not quite right. The rejection turned on sections 5.1, 11 and 17 fixing the COMPOSITION AND ORDER of the release; visibility surfaced in its question-7 answer as an aside, explicitly not ruled on. Nothing was left unsettled that the rejection needed to settle. The distinction matters because it changes what this proposal inherits: it inherits an open question that was correctly identified and correctly declined, not an unfinished ruling.

on_a_public_repository_has_no_reviewer.ruling: THEATRICAL, AND IT ARGUES AGAINST THE PROPOSAL'S OWN POSITION.
on_a_public_repository_has_no_reviewer.why: It is not true in the sense that matters: a public repository has MORE readers, not fewer, and that was the rejected amendment's argument for publishing early -- an argument the prior reviewer took seriously and marked down only for lacking evidence of an audience. The proposal cannot borrow the premise 'a public repository gets read' nowhere and then assert 'a public repository has no reviewer' as its closing line. What the sentence is groping toward is real and is stronger: publication is NOT REVERSIBLE IN SUBSTANCE. Forks, caches, archives and scrapes survive a re-privatisation, so unlike every other act in this project's rollback tables -- section 11 gives R1, R2 and R3 each an explicit rollback -- a visibility flip has no rollback. That is the honest form of the worry, it is specific, it is checkable, and it does the same rhetorical work without the flourish.
on_a_public_repository_has_no_reviewer.required: V4. Replace the closing sentence with the irreversibility point, or delete it. The paragraph is stronger without it: 'a flip made before those N files are read is a release of unreviewed prose' needs no help.

question_9_does_the_proposal_understate_.the_line_i_want_kept: 'Stated against my own preference: a public repository is what Ross wants and it is the outcome this project has been built toward.' Declaring the author's own interest before arguing against it is the right instinct and is what makes the rest of the document worth reading. Nothing in this ruling should be taken as discouraging it.

question_10_what_visibility_s_gate_shoul.the_ruling: VISIBILITY IS SEPARABLE FROM SECTION 17'S TWELVE EVIDENCE-ACCEPTANCE BOXES. IT IS NOT SEPARABLE FROM SECTION 2.1'S AUDIT NODE. Section 17 gates the RELEASE ARTIFACTS; section 2.1's 'licence, privacy and link audit' and section 3.1's naming of the repository as a canonical public artifact are what a visibility flip inherits.

why_section_17_does_not_gate_it.the_argument_from_the_boxes_own_content: Five of the twelve presuppose an object that does not exist for a bare repository and cannot be made to exist without building items 4-7: 'V1-V11 pass against ONE FROZEN RELEASE CANDIDATE'; 'Manifest, checksums and claim ledger are complete and immutable FOR THE RELEASE'; 'Adapter inference replay passes or adapter publication is removed'; 'GitHub, Hugging Face and Kaggle drafts are cross-linked and inspected'; 'Public V12 FRESH-DOWNLOAD verification passes and is recorded'. A checklist five of whose boxes are unsatisfiable-by-construction for an act is not a gate on that act. Applying it to visibility would mean the repository can only become readable after the entire seven-item release exists -- which is a coherent position, but it is a position no line of the plan states, and it would make section 12.4's 'pin ConformalExtract only after the public quickstart works' the plan's only acknowledgement of a state it never schedules.
why_section_17_does_not_gate_it.and_the_stages_confirm_it: Section 11 R3's five acts are all publications of artifacts; section 5.1's ten steps likewise. Neither names visibility. A plan that intended section 17 to gate visibility would have put visibility in R3.
why_section_17_does_not_gate_it.what_this_does_NOT_reopen: NOTHING about the seven-item minimum. The prior rejection stands in full: sections 5.1, 11 and 17 fix the composition and order of the RELEASE, items 5 and 6 are built and staged privately before the public act, and no staged A/B split is authorised. Separating visibility from section 17 makes the repository readable; it does not make anything released, does not tick a box, and does not shrink the seven.

the_gate_i_would_build_g1_to_g7.G1_plan_4_must_be_open: Plan 3 has no reviewer record carrying review_kind plan_close; CLAUDE.md's gated doctrine is 'Plan N+1 starts only after Plan N's independent reviewer PASS'; open-release-decisions.md's own closing line is 'Both items are gated behind Plan 4 opening, and Plan 4 has not opened'; README's Plan 4 row says 'not started'. A visibility flip is release execution. THIS GATE SITS ABOVE ALL THE OTHERS AND THE PROPOSAL DOES NOT NAME IT. Nothing below is reachable until it is satisfied, by whatever route the owner chooses (close Plan 3, or explicitly reduce scope under section 17's first line -- both are the owner's, both need a review).
